name: The shared grammar of tantric practice across the families

definitions.definition: Across the Śaiva, Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist and Jain tantras the same elements recur: initiation into a lineage and mantra; the mantra as the deity; the maṇḍala or yantra as the deity's seat and body; purification of the elements and installation of mantras on the body before worship; identification with the deity; the subtle body of channels and centres; the guru as the deity; secrecy and eligibility; and the twin aims of power (siddhi, bhukti) and liberation. Each family arranges them within its own view and goal.

The Mantramārga's ritual core: dīkṣā that destroys bonds, daily and occasional worship with nyāsa and bhūtaśuddhi, mantras as Śiva's body, and the sādhaka's pursuit of siddhis beside the liberation-seeker's path.
The Pāñcarātra saṃhitās, spoken by Nārāyaṇa, teach initiation, mantra, maṇḍala, nyāsa and temple worship as the means to reach the Lord; the Sātvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya are called its three gems.
The Mantranaya adds to the Mahāyāna path consecration, the deity's maṇḍala and mantra, and yoga with the channels, winds and drops, holding it swifter than the perfection vehicle.

Jain mantra-kalpas (Bhairava-Padmāvatī-kalpa, Jvālāmālinī-kalpa) teach the worship of the Jinas' attendant goddesses with seed syllables, yantras, body-protection and the six rites, for protection and worldly ends under devotion to the Jina; liberation stays the Jain liberation.

relations.note: the Buddhist fourfold/fivefold classification of tantras is one family's own ordering
the Trika's ranking of revelations orders the same features within Śaivism
initiation as the entry point of every tantric family

name: Enjoyment and liberation (bhukti–mukti; siddhi and mokṣa) as twin aims

definitions.definition: The Mantramārga distinguishes the initiate who seeks powers and enjoyments in higher worlds (bubhukṣu, the sādhaka) from the one who seeks liberation only (mumukṣu); both are legitimate and receive different initiations.
In the Kula way enjoyment itself becomes yoga: the yogin is not an enjoyer and the enjoyer does not know yoga, but the Kaula is both.
Common attainments (the eight great siddhis, the six rites) and the supreme attainment (mahāmudrā, buddhahood) are both fruits of mantra practice; the common are to be sought for the sake of beings.
Mantra rites for protection and worldly ends are practised under devotion to the Jina, while liberation comes only from the three jewels and the destruction of karma.

relations.note: same distinction of common and supreme attainment

name: Worshipping the deity by becoming the deity

definitions.definition: One who is not Śiva should not worship Śiva: the worshipper first makes himself Śiva by nyāsa and meditation ('śivo bhūtvā śivaṃ yajet').
The worshipper identifies with Viṣṇu before worshipping him (the same maxim with Viṣṇu's name appears in Vaiṣṇava ritual manuals).
In deity yoga the practitioner generates himself as the deity with its form, maṇḍala and 'divine pride', knowing the form to be empty.
The worshipper realizes identity with the Goddess in the Śrīcakra and in the body (the body as Śrīcakra).

relations.note: shared ritual logic; the Buddhist tradition insists the deity is empty of own nature while the Śaiva holds the self to be Śiva

notes: The maxims 'nādevo devam arcayet' / 'śivo bhūtvā śivaṃ yajet' are recalled from ritual manuals, not anchored to a verse here (no rests_on).

name: Installing mantras and letters on the body (nyāsa, sakalīkaraṇa)

definitions.definition: Before worship the body is made divine by placing mantras, the limbs (aṅga) of the deity's mantra and the letters of the alphabet on its parts.
Elaborate installations (e.g. the sixfold nyāsa) place the Goddess, her mantras and the letters on the body.
Syllables (oṃ āḥ hūṃ and the deity's seeds) are placed at the crown, throat and heart, and the body is seen as the deity's maṇḍala.
Jain worship begins with 'sakalīkaraṇa', protecting and consecrating the body by placing the syllables of the homage to the five supreme beings on the limbs.

relations.note: outer sites installed in the body (Buddhist)
the Jain five supreme beings as the content of the installation

notes: The Jain term sakalīkaraṇa (shared with Śaiva manuals) is recalled; flagged for checking.

name: The mantra as the deity's body

definitions.definition: Śiva's body is made of mantras (the five brahma-mantras as his faces); the mantra is the deity, not a name for it.
The deity arises from and dissolves into its seed syllable; the mantra is the deity's speech and essence.
The Namaskāra mantra is the embodiment of the five supreme beings and is meditated on as letters on lotuses in word-based meditation (padastha).
The mantra-manuals treat letters and seeds as the bodies of their deities.

name: The guru as the deity present in human form

definitions.definition: No god is beyond the guru and no mantra beyond his sandals; the guru is to be tested and so is the disciple.
The innate is known only from the true guru; without a guru there is no supreme siddhi.
Only one who has a guru drinks the nectar in the upturned well of the sky.
The true guru (satguru) gives the Name and is honoured above God as the means to him.

name: Secrecy and the qualified recipient across the tantric families

definitions.definition: The Kaula teaching is not to be given to one without devotion to the Kula and the guru or to a disciple only slightly tested.
The intentional language and the tantric teaching are not to be revealed to the unconsecrated.
Mantras given to one lacking the required qualities bear no fruit.

name: Transgressive practice and its inner reading, across families

definitions.definition: The Kula substances (wine, meat and the rest) are declared Śakti and Śiva and their union bliss; inner worship is dearer than outer; without the samaya discipline the wilful fall.
The haṭha texts quote the Kaula saying about eating cow's flesh and drinking the liquor of the immortals and read it as the tongue turned back into the skull and the nectar that flows there.
The Yoginī tantras give an intentional language of substitute words for substances, places and acts, not to be revealed to the unconsecrated; conduct in the cremation ground is for the qualified.

relations.note: the Kaula also teaches that the realized stands beyond rule; the inner reading is not the only one the texts give

notes: Summary level only; no ritual procedures are recorded (restricted material).

name: How the tantric families place their scriptures relative to the Veda or sūtras

definitions.definition: The Śaiva scriptures are a higher revelation than the Veda, which they do not contradict but surpass; the Veda is the lower, common scripture.
The Pāñcarātra is praised above all śāstras as the brahmin among the classes; its defenders (Yāmuna) argue that it is Vedic in root and authoritative.
The mantra way shares the goal of the perfection vehicle but is superior by its many means, lack of difficulty and suitability for the sharp.
Jain mantra lore is held to derive from the lost Vidyānupravāda Pūrva, part of the Jina's own canon, not from outside.

name: The two lists of eighty-four siddhas compared

definitions.definition: The Tibetan-transmitted list (Abhayadatta's Lives, Tōh 2292 songs) of eighty-four Buddhist siddhas — among them Lūipa, Virūpa, Saraha, Mīnapa, Gorakṣa, Cauraṅgī, Kāṇha, Jālandhara, Tilopa, Nāropa, and four women.

The Nāth tradition speaks of eighty-four siddhas and nine Nāths; its lists (e.g. the Haṭhapradīpikā's mahāsiddhas) mix Nāth names with names also found in the Buddhist list (Mīna, Cauraṅgī, Virūpākṣa, Carpaṭi, Kānerī).
A Maithili list of eighty-four (Varṇaratnākara, early 14th c.) mixes Nāth and Buddhist names.

members: shared names (in both traditions): Mīna/Matsyendra, Gorakṣa, Cauraṅgī, Jālandhara, Kāṇha, Virūpa/Virūpākṣa, Carpaṭi, Nāgārjuna
names only in the Buddhist list: Saraha, Lūipa, Tilopa, Nāropa, Maitrīpa and most others
names only in Nāth lists: Ādinātha, Gahinī, Revaṇa, Bhartṛhari, Gopīcandra and others

relations.note: the Buddhist list
the Nāth list
the Tamil count of eighteen, which also includes Korakkar (Gorakṣa)

notes: The number 84 is shared; the membership differs. The overlap is recorded as brw:natha-mahasiddha (U21) with U49 evidence.

name: Identifications of the same siddha across Nāth and Buddhist lists

definitions.definition: Several siddhas bear the same or cognate names in both traditions and share legends: Mīnapa and Matsyendra (Mīnanātha) both learn Śiva's secret teaching inside a fish; Jālandhara is Hāḍipā of the Bengali Nāth cycle and Jālandharipā of the Buddhist list, teacher of Kāṇha (Kānipā, Kāṇhapā); Cauraṅgī is the maimed prince restored in both; Gorakṣa appears in the Buddhist list as Cauraṅgī's cowherd attendant; Virūpa/Virūpākṣa is named in the Haṭhapradīpikā and credited in Tibet with the Amṛtasiddhi. Each tradition tells the stories within its own teaching.

members: Mīnapa = Matsyendra/Mīnanātha (identification held by some, distinguished by others)
notes: Whether Mīnapa and Matsyendra are one person is itself disputed in the traditions (the Tibetan lives make Mīnapa Matsyendra's father in some tellings) — recorded as an identification, not a fact.

name: The songs of the siddhas: dohā, caryā, vajragīti, sabad and pad

definitions.definition: Couplets (dohā) and rāga-set songs (caryā) in Apabhraṃśa and Old Bengali, signed by the siddha-poet, teach the innate in riddling images.
The Hindi sabadīs and pads ascribed to Gorakh and the Bengali Nāth song-cycles (Gopīcandra, Mayanāmatī) teach the yoga of the body in the same riddling register.
Kabīr's sākhīs (couplets) and pads continue the form, with the upside-down speech (ulaṭbāṃsī).

name: Coded and paradoxical speech across the families

definitions.definition: Intentional language (sandhyābhāṣā): substitute words for substances, places and acts, to be kept from the unconsecrated.
Upside-down speech: the upturned well in the sky, dying the sweet death.
Kaula etymologies and code-words give outer terms an inner yogic sense.
Ulaṭbāṃsī: Kabīr's paradox-riddles inherited from the Nāths.

name: The void (śūnya) as shared vocabulary of different referents

definitions.definition: The word śūnya/śūnyatā runs through Buddhist, Nāth, haṭha, Vīraśaiva and Sant language but names different things: for the Madhyamaka, the absence of own-nature in all dharmas; in the Buddhist completion stage, four graded 'empties' leading to clear light; in the haṭha texts, the central channel (śūnyapadavī) and the voids pierced in the four stages; for the Nāths and Allama, the fullness beyond the mind; for the Sants, the sky-circle where the Name resounds.

relations.note: Madhyamaka emptiness is a negation of own-nature, not a place or state reached in the body
Buddhist completion-stage series

name: Reversing the downward flow: the upward current in the body

definitions.definition: The moon's nectar, consumed by the sun below, is to be kept and turned back; the breath is forced into the central channel.
The fire of caṇḍālī at the navel melts the moon at the head; the drops descend through the four joys and are drawn back upward.
The reversal (ulṭā) of the current to the sky-circle where the nectar dwells.
The upstream journey (ujān) against the current, to the source.

notes: Summary only; sexual and retention practices associated with the theme are restricted and not described.

name: The subtle body across the families: differing counts of channels and centres

definitions.definition: Three principal channels (lalanā, rasanā, avadhūtī) among thirty-two; four (or five, six in the Kālacakra) wheels.
Six (or nine) centres, sixteen supports, three targets and five voids; the bulb below the navel from which 72,000 channels arise.
Eleven centres or kinds of inner knowledge in the Kaulajñānanirṇaya; the worlds located in the body as principles.
The Netra's six wheels, sixteen supports, three targets and five voids.
Word-based meditation places the vowels and consonants on lotuses at the navel, heart and mouth; the Jain texts do not teach the Śaiva centres as such.

notes: The counts differ by text and are not to be harmonized in the text layer; the map is interpretive.

name: The sacred seats shared by Kaula, Nāth and Buddhist tantras

definitions.definition: Oḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Pūrṇagiri and Kāmarūpa as the primary seats; Bhairava present with the Goddess at Kāmākhyā where the yoginīs meet.
The twenty-four sites of the Heruka maṇḍala (Pullīramalaya, Jālandhara, Oḍḍiyāna, Arbuda, Devīkoṭa, Kāmarūpa …) and the Hevajra's ten classes of sites (pīṭha, upapīṭha …), mapped onto the body.
Kāmarūpa placed between the first two centres in the Gorakṣaśataka; Jālandhara as a siddha's name and a seat.

relations.note: the later Purāṇic network of 51 seats from Satī's body has another origin story

name: Tārā in the Buddhist and Hindu tantras

definitions.definition: Tārā, the saviouress who ferries beings across dangers, a female buddha or bodhisattva of compassion; forms include Green and White Tārā and the fierce Ekajaṭā and Mahācīna-Tārā, the latter crowned with Akṣobhya.
Tārā is the second of the ten Mahāvidyās, fierce and dark blue, with Akṣobhya on her head; her Kula worship is said to have been learned in Mahācīna from the Buddha by Vasiṣṭha.

notes: The Hindu texts themselves narrate the Buddhist connection (brw:tara-mahacina-buddhist).

name: The six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅga) in its several forms

definitions.definition: Maitrī Upaniṣad: breath-control, withdrawal, meditation, concentration, reasoning (tarka) and absorption; the Amṛtanāda lists the same six in another order.
The Śaiva Mantramārga teaches a six-limbed yoga with reasoning (tarka) as a limb (Mṛgendra's yoga section: breath-control, withdrawal, concentration, meditation, reasoning, absorption).
Guhyasamāja and Kālacakra: withdrawal, meditation, breath-control, retention, recollection (anusmṛti) and absorption — the completion-stage yoga of the Kālacakra.
Gorakṣaśataka and Vivekamārtaṇḍa: posture, breath-control, withdrawal, concentration, meditation, absorption (the yamas and niyamas not counted).

relations.note: tarka as the limb distinguishing the Upaniṣadic and Śaiva lists

notes: Same names in different orders with different contents and goals; the Kālacakra tradition defines each limb by its own signs. See brw:sadanga-yoga-shared-limbs (U44) and brw:sadanga-yoga-maitri-to-mantramarga (U49).

name: Reasoning (tarka) as a limb of yoga

definitions.definition: In the Maitrī's six limbs reasoning stands between concentration and absorption.
The Śaiva ṣaḍaṅga counts tarka — the discernment of what is to be taken up and left — as the highest limb (Mālinīvijayottara, recalled; Mṛgendra's yoga section).

relations.note: Patañjali's eight limbs have no tarka

name: The four immeasurables / attitudes across Buddhist, Yoga and Jain teaching

definitions.definition: Love, compassion, rejoicing and equanimity pervading all directions without measure; the Buddha says other wanderers teach the same but cannot say where each culminates (the beautiful, infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness).
Friendliness, compassion, gladness and equanimity toward the happy, the suffering, the virtuous and the non-virtuous clear the mind.
Friendliness toward all beings, joy (pramoda) toward the more virtuous, compassion toward the afflicted and impartiality (mādhyasthya) toward the unruly, as supporting reflections of the vows.

relations.note: the Buddhist form pervades all directions without assigning classes of objects; the Yoga and Jain forms assign each attitude an object-class

notes: Structural observation (interpretation layer): YS 1.33 and TS 7.11 both pair each attitude with a class of beings; the Pali formula does not.

name: The five restraints as 'great vow' across Jain, Yoga and Brahmanical renunciation

definitions.definition: Abstention from violence, falsehood, stealing, unchastity and possessiveness is the vow; kept in part it is the small vow, in full the great vow (mahāvrata) of the mendicant.
The same five are the yamas; unlimited by birth, place, time or occasion they are the great vow (mahāvrata).
The Dharmasūtras give the renouncer a set of vows of the same kind (non-injury, truth, not stealing, celibacy, renunciation).
The five lay precepts overlap (non-killing, non-stealing, sexual restraint, truthful speech) but replace non-possession with abstention from intoxicants.

relations.note: the Terāpanth's distinction is a later Jain development

notes: The list and the term mahāvrata are identical in Jain and Yoga texts (see brw:jain-mahavratas-and-yoga-yamas). The Dharmasūtra list is recalled at chapter level.

name: Levels of truth across the families (two truths, three levels, niścaya–vyavahāra)

definitions.definition: The Buddhas teach relying on two truths, worldly convention and the ultimate.

Gauḍapāda distinguishes what exists by imagined or dependent convention from the ultimate, and the worldly, pure-worldly and supramundane; later Advaita counts three levels (ultimate, empirical, illusory); Śrīharṣa says the Brahma-vādin differs from the Mādhyamika in exempting consciousness.
The Jains speak of the ultimate and conventional standpoints (niścaya- and vyavahāra-naya) within a many-sided view.

relations.note: the reconciling principle P1 itself; the Advaita tradition holds the ultimate to be the self-luminous Brahman, the Madhyamaka holds it to be emptiness — the tradition of each rejects the other's ultimate

name: Placing the other schools as lower stages of one's own

definitions.definition: All philosophies are roles of the one conscious Lord: Buddhists rest in the intellect-principle, Jains in the qualities, Vedic knowers in the Person, Pāñcarātrikas in the unmanifest; the Trika alone sees the self as both transcendent and immanent.
Mādhava's compendium arranges sixteen systems from the Cārvāka upward ending in Advaita; Madhusūdana holds that all sages intend the one Lord and their differing paths suit differing capacities.

Haribhadra sets out six darśanas without polemic; Siddhasena holds that there are as many doctrines as ways of speaking, and that the Jina's word is the aggregate of all the one-sided views; the Sūtrakṛtāṅga tradition classes rival doctrines as 363 kinds of kriyāvāda, akriyāvāda, ajñāna and vinaya.
The Brahmajāla surveys the ascetics' and brahmins' theories about past and future on sixty-two grounds, all arising from contact and feeling, which the Tathāgata knows and goes beyond.
Bhāviveka examines the Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Vedānta and Mīmāṃsā and grants what is acceptable in the Vedānta only as the emptiness the Buddha taught.

notes: Each such ranking is one tradition's view (see dsp:ranking-of-other-revelations); being ranked lower is rejected by the ranked tradition.

name: Subordinating another family's deities or founder

definitions.definition: Vajrapāṇi as Trailokyavijaya subdues Maheśvara and the worldly gods and gives them places in the maṇḍala; Heruka's taking of the twenty-four sites is told as the conversion of Bhairava's retinue.
Viṣṇu sends forth the Great Deluder, who teaches the daityas the doctrines of the naked and the red-robed ascetics so that they abandon the Veda.
The Buddha appears as a Kula-Bhairava perfected by Tārā's mantra, the teacher of Vasiṣṭha.
Kṛṣṇa and Rāma are retold as figures within the Jain universal history, subordinate to the Jinas.

name: Yoga declared independent of sect and outward sign

definitions.definition: Brahmin, śramaṇa, Buddhist, Jain, Kāpālika or materialist — whoever practises with faith attains success; garb and sectarian formulas are not the cause of success.
Haribhadra correlates the eight views of the yoga-seeker with the limbs beginning with yama, treating yoga taught under other names as one path of qualities.
Hindu and Turk quarrel over names; neither knows the secret.

name: The shared framework of means of knowledge and debate

definitions.definition: The means of knowledge, the five-membered demonstration, pseudo-reasons and points of defeat; Uddyotakara writes to remove the errors of 'bad reasoners' (the Buddhists).
Two means of knowledge, inference with the three characteristics of the reason; answers to the Jain single-mark theory.
The single mark of a valid reason is 'otherwise-impossibility' (anyathānupapatti); Jain logic adopts and revises the Nyāya and Buddhist frameworks.

name: The three humours in Āyurveda, Tibetan medicine and Siddha medicine

definitions.definition: Vāta, pitta and kapha, which sustain the body in balance and cause disease when disturbed.
Wind (rlung), bile (mkhris pa) and phlegm (bad kan), which the Four Tantras trace to the three mental poisons — desire, hatred and delusion — rooted in ignorance.
Vaḷi, aḻal and aiyam (the three kuṟṟam).

relations.note: the Tibetan system adds the root in the three poisons

notes: The Tibetan tradition's own debate on whether the Four Tantras are the Buddha's word is recorded by U48 as dsp:gyushi-buddha-word; the borrowing is brw:ayurveda-to-sowa-rigpa.

name: The Sant, Bāul and Sufi exchanges (context only)

definitions.definition: Kabīr addresses Hindu and Turk alike, rejects both their rites, and uses Persian and Sufi words (pīr, the beloved, the lover's pain) beside Nāth and Vaiṣṇava ones. Recorded as context only.
Bāuls and Fakirs share gurus, songs and practice; Lalon sings of the original Mecca in the human body. Context only.
Dārā Shikoh's Persian Upaniṣads (Sirr-i Akbar, 1657) and his comparative Majmaʿ al-Baḥrayn (1655), with his recorded questions to Bābā Lāl, are documents of the exchange. Context only.

notes: Sufism is outside the ontology's scope: no Sufi lineage, doctrine or teaching is recorded; only the in-scope side of the exchange and the documents that witness it.

name: The cloud of dharma (dharmamegha)

definitions.definition: Dharmameghā ('cloud of dharma') is the name of the tenth bodhisattva ground, on which the bodhisattva is consecrated by the buddhas' rays and rains the dharma on beings like a cloud.

relations.note: same name, different referent: in Yoga a samādhi of complete discernment before kaivalya (YS 4.29), in the Mahāyāna the last bodhisattva ground before buddhahood; historical relation disputed (brw:mahayana-yoga-dharmamegha)

name: The five faculties and five powers

definitions.definition: For those not born into the state, asaṃprajñāta samādhi is preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, samādhi and insight, each giving rise to the next.

relations.note: identical list of five; Yoga orders them as a causal sequence toward seedless samādhi, Buddhism as balanced faculties toward liberation

name: Non-origination (ajātivāda)

definitions.definition: No existent arises from itself, from another, from both or without cause (MMK 1.1); non-arising (anutpāda) is the emptiness of own-nature, not the unborn self.

relations.note: Gauḍapāda's non-origination is of the non-dual self; the Madhyamaka's is of all dharmas without a remaining self — the Advaita tradition insists on the difference (GK 4.99)

name: The four pādas: caryā, kriyā, yoga, jñāna

definitions.definition: Several Pāñcarātra saṃhitās (e.g. the Pādma) are likewise divided into four quarters — knowledge, yoga, ritual and conduct.

notes: U49 contribution: the four-quarter division is shared by Śaiva Āgamas and Pāñcarātra saṃhitās (brw:saiva-siddhanta-pancaratra).

name: Buddha-nature and the Upaniṣadic self: the question of likeness

definitions.definition: The Mahāparinirvāṇa calls the tathāgatagarbha the 'self' of beings and the Ratnagotravibhāga counts self among the four perfections of the fruit; the Laṅkāvatāra raises the objection that this is like the tīrthakaras' self and answers that it is taught as a skilful name for emptiness, to attract those who cling to a self.
The self (ātman) of the Upaniṣads is permanent, unborn and the inner controller, known as one's own being.

relations.note: the Laṅkāvatāra distinguishes the tathāgatagarbha from any permanent agent-self; the Buddhist tradition insists on the difference (P6-upaya is its own principle)

notes: The tradition of each side rejects identity: recorded as a question of likeness, not as an equivalence. See dsp:buddha-nature-self-or-emptiness and brw:tathagatagarbha-and-atman.

name: Meru and Jambudvīpa: the shared cosmography of the families

definitions.definition: Seven ring-continents and oceans around Jambudvīpa, with Meru at its centre and Bhārata as the land of action.
Jambūdvīpa, round, a hundred thousand yojanas across, with Meru as its navel, surrounded by continents and oceans; Bharata and Airāvata as regions of the six-period cycles.
The receptacle world on circles of wind, water and gold; Meru amid seven golden ranges, with four continents, Jambudvīpa to the south.
Vyāsa's cosmology of seven worlds from Avīci to the back of Meru and above.

notes: Same names (Meru, Jambudvīpa, Bhārata) with different geometries in each family.

name: Cycles of cosmic time across the families

definitions.definition: Four ages (kṛta, tretā, dvāpara, kali) making a mahāyuga; a day of Brahmā (kalpa) and its night of dissolution.
Endless alternation of ascending and descending half-cycles (utsarpiṇī, avasarpiṇī), each of six periods, in Bharata and Airāvata.
Aeons (kalpa) of formation, duration, destruction and emptiness; the great aeon made of eighty intermediate aeons.

notes: 'kalpa' is shared vocabulary with different measures and structures.
